chapterTitle: Spam and Virus Filtering with Postfix and Amavisd-new/SpamAssassin

screens.title: Spam and Virus Filtering with Postfix and Amavisd-new/SpamAssassin
screens.narratorSegment: Email servers without content filtering quickly become noisy, insecure, and unusable. In this lesson you will learn why layered filtering matters, how Amavisd-new mediates between Postfix and scanners, and what practical steps to take to install, configure, and verify SpamAssassin and ClamAV. We’ll emphasize reliable handoff using Postfix’s content_filter and the complementary listener in master. cf, configuring amavisd. conf thresholds and actions, and the correct service start order to avoid bypass. You will see concrete command examples for installation, a real configuration example for Postfix and amavisd, and the safe test procedures using the GTUBE and EICAR test strings. By the end you will be able to assemble a working pipeline, interpret relevant logs to confirm behavior, and identify common misconfigurations such as incorrect socket paths or missing content_filter entries. Think of Amavisd-new as a translator: Postfix speaks SMTP, scanners speak scan protocols, and Amavisd-new accepts mail, queries SpamAssassin and ClamAV, and returns a definitive instruction to Postfix. That translation is what keeps malicious or unwanted mail from reaching users. As you start, consider what policy you want for quarantines and rejections, because amavisd. conf will enforce those decisions.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: These four objectives map to the practical steps you will perform and the reasoning behind them. First, you will understand why anti-spam and anti-virus layers are necessary: they reduce noise, prevent compromise, and protect reputation. Second, you will integrate Amavisd-new with Postfix so mail is reliably handed off and returned after scanning. Third, you will configure Amavisd-new to call SpamAssassin and ClamAV with sensible thresholds and socket settings so the system takes the correct action on spam and malware. Fourth, you will implement basic quarantine and notification settings and learn how to troubleshoot filtering by examining service logs and looking for common misconfigurations. For each objective we include a short explanation and a small mnemonic so you can remember the sequence: detect, decide, act, verify. These skills are practical: you will run package installs, change Postfix main. cf and master. cf, edit amavisd. conf, and run safe tests using GTUBE and the EICAR test file. By the end, you will be able to assemble and verify a production-ready filtering pipeline and interpret log entries to confirm the policy is applied.

screens.title: Mail flow: Postfix ↔ Amavisd-new ↔ Scanners
screens.narratorSegment: Understanding the mail flow is the foundation for configuring filtering correctly. Conceptually, Postfix receives incoming SMTP sessions and, when content_filter is set, hands the message to Amavisd-new by opening an SMTP connection to the Amavisd listener. Amavisd-new then invokes SpamAssassin for content scoring and an anti-virus scanner such as ClamAV to inspect attachments. Based on configured thresholds and actions in amavisd. conf, Amavisd-new decides whether to tag, quarantine, reject, or pass the message and then re-injects the message back into Postfix on a dedicated listener, typically 127.0.0.1:10025. That listener is configured in master. cf with relaxed recipient checks because the mail originated from a trusted local scanner process. A common misconception is that Amavisd-new permanently stores mail: it does not by default; it returns instructions to Postfix which then performs the actual delivery or rejection. For secure operation, ensure sockets and ports used by ClamAV and Amavisd-new match exactly, and keep network policy strict so only localhost can access the scanned-mail listener. As a practical mental model, think: receive, scan, decide, return — and make sure each arrow in that chain is configured and reachable.

keyIdea.title: Four-step mail pipeline
keyIdea.text: Postfix hands off, Amavisd-new runs SpamAssassin and ClamAV, then returns the message and an action to Postfix for final delivery.

content.html:
Module 05 › Chapter 5.6 › Mail flow
Process Flow
The reliable handoff requires two Postfix endpoints: the outbound content_filter target where Postfix sends unsifted mail to Amavisd-new, and a returning listener (127.0.0.1:10025) where scanned mail arrives for final delivery or further SMTP processing.
1. Postfix receives SMTP and sends to Amavisd-new via content_filter at 127.0.0.1:10024.
2. Amavisd-new invokes SpamAssassin and ClamAV; collects scores and findings.
3. Amavisd-new decides action (pass, quarantine, reject) and returns mail to Postfix on 127.0.0.1:10025.
4. Postfix performs final delivery using relaxed checks for the trusted source.
Common misconception
Amavisd-new is not a mail store. It scans and instructs Postfix; configure Postfix listeners correctly so mail is not bypassed or dropped.
Diagram — boxed steps
Postfix (inbound)
content_filter => 127.0.0.1:10024
Ensure content_filter is present in /etc/postfix/main.cf or mail will bypass scanning.
Amavisd-new
Calls SpamAssassin and ClamAV
Match ClamAV socket configured in clamd to the socket referenced in amavisd.conf.
Returning listener
127.0.0.1:10025 in master.cf with relaxed checks

Module 05 › Chapter 5.6 › Install
Commands (RHEL/CentOS)
sudo dnf install amavisd-new spamassassin clamav clamd -y
sudo systemctl enable --now amavisd
sudo systemctl enable --now spamassassin   # may be spamd on some systems
sudo systemctl enable --now clamd@scan
sudo freshclam
Verify the services are active. If freshclam reports errors, resolve networking or DNS before continuing. Confirm service names because they vary between distributions.
Verification checklist
  • systemctl status clamd@scan, amavisd, and spamassassin/spamd show active.
  • freshclam completes and updates virus definitions.
  • Server DNS resolution works for SpamAssassin network tests.
Pro tip
If your system uses a different clamd socket path, note it now; you will reference it when editing amavisd.conf.

screens.title: Configure Postfix to use Amavisd-new
screens.narratorSegment: Configuring Postfix to hand mail to Amavisd-new is accomplished by adding a content_filter entry in main. cf and a matching listener in master. cf. The content_filter line tells Postfix to open an SMTP connection to the Amavisd feed endpoint. Amavisd-new typically listens on 127.0.0.1:10024 for incoming mail handed off by Postfix and then returns scanned mail to 127.0.0.1:10025. In master. cf you add a 127.0.0.1:10025 listener with a set of -o overrides that relax recipient checks because the mail has already been scanned and originates from a trusted local source. A common mistake is forgetting to reload Postfix after edits or misindenting master. cf entries; master. cf is sensitive to tabs for the service lines. After editing, reload Postfix, send a test message, and watch the logs to confirm the handoff. If mail is still bypassing filtering, the most likely cause is a missing or commented out content_filter line in main. cf. Always backup configuration files before changing them so you can revert quickly. keyIdea.text: Set content_filter in main.cf and add a 127.0.0.1:10025 master.cf listener with relaxed checks for scanned mail reinjection.

content.html:
Module 05 › Chapter 5.6 › Postfix Configuration
/etc/postfix/main.cf
# /etc/postfix/main.cf
# Set Amavisd-new as the content filter for incoming mail
content_filter = amavisfeed:[127.0.0.1]:10024

# Example existing milter entry preserved if present
smtpd_milters = unix:/var/run/opendkim/opendkim.sock
Add the content_filter line and save. Next, add the master.cf service on 127.0.0.1:10025 to receive scanned mail back from Amavisd-new.
/etc/postfix/master.cf (snippet)
# Service for Postfix to receive scanned mail from Amavisd-new
127.0.0.1:10025 inet    n       -       y       -       -       smtpd
    -o content_filter=
    -o receive_override_options=no_unknown_recipient_checks,no_header_body_checks
    -o smtpd_recipient_restrictions=permit_mynetworks,reject
    -o mynetworks=127.0.0.0/8
    -o smtpd_delay_reject=no
    -o smtpd_tls_security_level=may
    -o smtpd_authorized_xforward_hosts=127.0.0.0/8
Remember: use tabs to align master.cf columns. Reload Postfix after editing with a safe backup in place.

screens.title: Key amavisd.conf settings
screens.narratorSegment: Amavisd-new’s behavior is controlled by variables in amavisd. conf. Important arrays such as @bypass_virus_checks_maps and @bypass_spam_checks_maps allow you to whitelist senders or recipients. Spam thresholds are set with variables like $sa_tag_level_temp, $sa_tag_level_kill, and $sa_quarantine_cutoff_level; these determine when headers are added, when mail is treated as spam, and when it is quarantined or bounced. Action variables such as $final_virus_lovers and $final_spam_lovers define the final disposition: pass, discard, or reject. For ClamAV integration, Amavisd-new contains entries like 'ClamAV-clamd' using ask_daemon and a socket path; this must match the LocalSocket or TCP settings in clamd. conf. A frequent misconfiguration is mismatched socket paths; if amavisd. conf points to /var/run/clamd. scan/clamd. sock but clamd is bound to /run/clamd. scan/clamd. sock or a TCP port, scans fail silently or return errors. Keep spam and virus thresholds deliberate: a low kill threshold will bounce many messages; a higher quarantine threshold allows investigation. Always restart services after changing amavisd. conf and monitor logs for errors pointing to syntax or socket problems. Key amavisd.conf settings means set spamassassin thresholds and ensure clamav socket paths in amavisd.conf match clamd configuration to avoid scan failures.. In practical terms, spam thresholds, action variables, and clamav integration. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Tune thresholds and sockets
keyIdea.text: Set SpamAssassin thresholds and ensure ClamAV socket paths in amavisd.conf match clamd configuration to avoid scan failures.

content.html:
Module 05 › Chapter 5.6 › Amavisd-new Configuration
SpamAssassin thresholds
$sa_tag_level_temp = -999; # add spam info headers if spam score >= -999
$sa_tag_level_kill = 6.31; # treat as spam if score >= 6.31
$sa_quarantine_cutoff_level = 6.31; # quarantine if score >= 6.31
$sa_dsn_cutoff_level = 10; # bounce if score >= 10
Adjust these values to match your tolerance for false positives. Document any changes and notify user support if thresholds change.
ClamAV integration
['ClamAV-clamd',
  \&ask_daemon, ["CONTSCAN {}
", "/var/run/clamd.scan/clamd.sock"],
  qr/\bOK$/, qr/\bFOUND$/]
Confirm the socket path here matches clamd.conf LocalSocket, or use 127.0.0.1:3310 for TCP connections where appropriate.
$final_virus_lovers
Set to D_REJECT to reject infected mail, D_DISCARD to drop, or D_PASS to allow delivery with warnings.
Whitelist maps
Use @bypass_virus_checks_maps and @bypass_spam_checks_maps to whitelist trusted senders or internal systems.
Logging & errors
After edits, restart amavisd and check journalctl -u amavisd for socket or syntax problems.

screens.title: Service order and socket pitfalls
screens.narratorSegment: Service start order and matching socket configuration are frequent causes of broken filtering. ClamAV and SpamAssassin must be running before Amavisd-new starts so Amavisd can connect to the scanners at launch. If Amavisd-new starts first and the scanner sockets are absent, Amavisd may log errors and fail to scan mail. The recommended restart order is: start or restart clamd (or clamd@scan), then spamassassin or spamd, then amavisd, and finally reload Postfix so it can send new mail through the content_filter. Another common pitfall is mismatched socket paths: clamd. conf defines LocalSocket or TCPSocket; that exact value must be referenced in amavisd. conf. If you see connection refused or missing socket errors in amavisd logs, confirm the socket path and permissions and check that the clamd socket file exists and is readable by the amavisd user. If you must run ClamAV on TCP, use 127.0.0.1:3310 in amavisd. conf. Also ensure firewall rules do not block loopback TCP if you rely on TCP sockets. Always inspect journalctl and maillog entries after restarts to detect timing issues. Service order and socket pitfalls means start clamav and spamassassin before amavisd-new; verify socket paths and permissions to avoid scan failures.. In practical terms, start-up sequencing, socket paths, and common errors. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

GTUBE spam test
echo "X5O!P%@AP[4\\PZX54(P^)7CC)7}$EICAR-STANDARD-ANTIVIRUS-TEST-FILE!$H+H*" | mail -s "GTUBE Test" mailuser1@your_domain.com
This should trigger SpamAssassin and either tag or quarantine the message depending on your amavisd.conf settings.
EICAR virus test
echo 'X5O!P%@AP[4\\PZX54(P^)7CC)7}$EICAR-STANDARD-ANTIVIRUS-TEST-FILE!$H+H*' > eicar.com
# send with mutt or your mail client attaching eicar.com

Inspect logs: sudo journalctl -u amavisd or tail -n 200 /var/log/maillog to find ClamAV detections and the resulting action.
What to look for in logs
  • X-Spam-Flag or X-Spam-Score headers added by Amavisd-new/SpamAssassin.

screens.title: Quarantine, reject, or pass?
screens.narratorSegment: Choosing what to do with flagged mail depends on organizational risk tolerance and user expectations. For viruses, many administrators choose to reject infected mail outright by setting $final_virus_lovers to D_REJECT, because allowing infected attachments into inboxes risks compromise. For spam, options vary: you can tag and deliver, quarantine for administrator review, discard silently, or bounce. Use $sa_tag_level_kill and $sa_quarantine_cutoff_level to control when items are treated as spam and when they are quarantined. A typical mistake is setting aggressive thresholds that create many false positives; this harms users and increases support burden. Another mistake is over-trusting whitelists, which let potentially malicious mail bypass checks. A balanced policy is to quarantine high-scoring spam and tag medium scores so users can see warnings. Ensure quarantine notifications and retention policies are documented so administrators can find and restore mail if necessary. Whatever you choose, test the policy with GTUBE and EICAR and inspect logs to confirm the action is enforced. Quarantine, reject, or pass? means reject viruses to minimize risk; tune spam thresholds to balance false positives and operational workload; test policies with gtube and eicar.. In practical terms, choosing actions for spam and virus detections. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 05 › Chapter 5.6 › Policy Decisions
Virus actions (recommended)
Set $final_virus_lovers to D_REJECT to refuse infected messages at SMTP time. This prevents harmful files from ever reaching mailboxes or quarantine storage that might be accidentally reintroduced.
Spam actions (options)
Lower scores: tag headers and deliver with notice. Medium scores: quarantine for admin review. High scores: discard or reject depending on tolerance for false positives.
Risks
  • Aggressive thresholds produce false positives and user complaints.
  • Overuse of whitelists can allow malicious mail through.
  • Poor quarantine notification confuses administrators.
Key takeaway
Document and test your policy. Use GTUBE and EICAR to verify actions, and ensure logs show the intended disposition.

screens.title: Troubleshoot filtering failures
screens.narratorSegment: When filtering doesn't work, a methodical checklist reduces time to resolution. First, confirm services are running: systemctl status for clamd, spamassassin or spamd, and amavisd. Second, check Postfix main. cf to ensure content_filter is present; without it, Postfix will not send mail to Amavisd-new. Third, inspect master. cf for the returning listener on 127.0.0.1:10025 to ensure scanned mail is accepted back into Postfix with relaxed checks. Fourth, examine amavisd logs via journalctl -u amavisd for socket or syntax errors and maillog or journalctl for Postfix handoff and re-injection events. Fifth, verify ClamAV socket path and permissions; use ls -l on the socket file and match it to the path in amavisd. conf. Sixth, verify DNS resolution; SpamAssassin uses network lookups and may fail to apply rules without working DNS. Common mistakes include forgetting to reload Postfix after config changes, using the wrong socket path in amavisd. conf, and starting services in the wrong order. Work through the checklist, re-run tests, and keep a copy of original configurations for rollback. Troubleshoot filtering failures means verify daemons, content_filter, master.cf listener, socket paths, permissions, dns, and logs to find and fix filtering failures.. In practical terms, check logs, sockets, content_filter, and service status. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. fullNarratorScript:
Email servers without content filtering quickly become noisy, insecure, and unusable. In this lesson you will learn why layered filtering matters, how Amavisd-new mediates between Postfix and scanners, and what practical steps to take to install, configure, and verify SpamAssassin and ClamAV. We’ll emphasize reliable handoff using Postfix’s content_filter and the complementary listener in master. cf, configuring amavisd. conf thresholds and actions, and the correct service start order to avoid bypass. You will see concrete command examples for installation, a real configuration example for Postfix and amavisd, and the safe test procedures using the GTUBE and EICAR test strings. By the end you will be able to assemble a working pipeline, interpret relevant logs to confirm behavior, and identify common misconfigurations such as incorrect socket paths or missing content_filter entries. Think of Amavisd-new as a translator: Postfix speaks SMTP, scanners speak scan protocols, and Amavisd-new accepts mail, queries SpamAssassin and ClamAV, and returns a definitive instruction to Postfix. That translation is what keeps malicious or unwanted mail from reaching users. As you start, consider what policy you want for quarantines and rejections, because amavisd. conf will enforce those decisions.

These four objectives map to the practical steps you will perform and the reasoning behind them. First, you will understand why anti-spam and anti-virus layers are necessary: they reduce noise, prevent compromise, and protect reputation. Second, you will integrate Amavisd-new with Postfix so mail is reliably handed off and returned after scanning. Third, you will configure Amavisd-new to call SpamAssassin and ClamAV with sensible thresholds and socket settings so the system takes the correct action on spam and malware. Fourth, you will implement basic quarantine and notification settings and learn how to troubleshoot filtering by examining service logs and looking for common misconfigurations. For each objective we include a short explanation and a small mnemonic so you can remember the sequence: detect, decide, act, verify. These skills are practical: you will run package installs, change Postfix main. cf and master. cf, edit amavisd. conf, and run safe tests using GTUBE and the EICAR test file. By the end, you will be able to assemble and verify a production-ready filtering pipeline and interpret log entries to confirm the policy is applied.

In this second objectives panel we break the practical tasks into repeatable steps you will do during the hands-on portion. You will install amavisd-new, SpamAssassin, and ClamAV using your system package manager and enable the daemons for persistent operation. Next, you will modify Postfix main. cf to set the content_filter to the Amavisd-new inlet and add a corresponding listener in master. cf so scanned mail returns on port 10025. Then you will edit amavisd. conf to confirm spam thresholds, quarantine levels, and the ClamAV socket or TCP address. Finally, you will run safe tests using the GTUBE and EICAR strings and read the logs to confirm actions. Each step includes verification: service status, freshclam update results, and maillog or journalctl entries. This sequence ensures you not only change files but also observe evidence that the pipeline is working. Practicing these steps builds confidence and reduces the chance of mail bypass due to common misconfiguration.

Understanding the mail flow is the foundation for configuring filtering correctly. Conceptually, Postfix receives incoming SMTP sessions and, when content_filter is set, hands the message to Amavisd-new by opening an SMTP connection to the Amavisd listener. Amavisd-new then invokes SpamAssassin for content scoring and an anti-virus scanner such as ClamAV to inspect attachments. Based on configured thresholds and actions in amavisd. conf, Amavisd-new decides whether to tag, quarantine, reject, or pass the message and then re-injects the message back into Postfix on a dedicated listener, typically 127.0.0.1:10025. That listener is configured in master. cf with relaxed recipient checks because the mail originated from a trusted local scanner process. A common misconception is that Amavisd-new permanently stores mail: it does not by default; it returns instructions to Postfix which then performs the actual delivery or rejection. For secure operation, ensure sockets and ports used by ClamAV and Amavisd-new match exactly, and keep network policy strict so only localhost can access the scanned-mail listener. As a practical mental model, think: receive, scan, decide, return — and make sure each arrow in that chain is configured and reachable.

Installation is the first practical step and must be verified before configuration. On Red Hat-based systems you install the three building blocks: amavisd-new, SpamAssassin, and ClamAV including the clamd daemon. After installation, enable and start clamd, spamassassin or spamd, and amavisd in the correct sequence so Amavisd-new can connect to those services at boot. Run freshclam to fetch the latest signature definitions for ClamAV immediately. A common point of confusion is service names: SpamAssassin may run as spamassassin or as spamd depending on the distribution, and clamd may be presented as a templated service like clamd@scan. After enabling, check service status and ensure freshclam completes without network errors. If freshclam fails, ClamAV will still run but will not detect recent threats. Also ensure your server has working DNS because SpamAssassin uses DNS for RBL and network tests. The code block shows installation and enabling commands you will type. After this step, we move to Postfix integration with content_filter. Install Amavisd-new, SpamAssassin, and ClamAV means install packages, enable daemons, and run freshclam so signature updates are current before integrating with postfix.. In practical terms, commands to install and enable required services on rhel-based systems. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Configuring Postfix to hand mail to Amavisd-new is accomplished by adding a content_filter entry in main. cf and a matching listener in master. cf. The content_filter line tells Postfix to open an SMTP connection to the Amavisd feed endpoint. Amavisd-new typically listens on 127.0.0.1:10024 for incoming mail handed off by Postfix and then returns scanned mail to 127.0.0.1:10025. In master. cf you add a 127.0.0.1:10025 listener with a set of -o overrides that relax recipient checks because the mail has already been scanned and originates from a trusted local source. A common mistake is forgetting to reload Postfix after edits or misindenting master. cf entries; master. cf is sensitive to tabs for the service lines. After editing, reload Postfix, send a test message, and watch the logs to confirm the handoff. If mail is still bypassing filtering, the most likely cause is a missing or commented out content_filter line in main. cf. Always backup configuration files before changing them so you can revert quickly. Amavisd-new’s behavior is controlled by variables in amavisd. conf. Important arrays such as @bypass_virus_checks_maps and @bypass_spam_checks_maps allow you to whitelist senders or recipients. Spam thresholds are set with variables like $sa_tag_level_temp, $sa_tag_level_kill, and $sa_quarantine_cutoff_level; these determine when headers are added, when mail is treated as spam, and when it is quarantined or bounced. Action variables such as $final_virus_lovers and $final_spam_lovers define the final disposition: pass, discard, or reject. For ClamAV integration, Amavisd-new contains entries like 'ClamAV-clamd' using ask_daemon and a socket path; this must match the LocalSocket or TCP settings in clamd. conf. A frequent misconfiguration is mismatched socket paths; if amavisd. conf points to /var/run/clamd. scan/clamd. sock but clamd is bound to /run/clamd. scan/clamd. sock or a TCP port, scans fail silently or return errors. Keep spam and virus thresholds deliberate: a low kill threshold will bounce many messages; a higher quarantine threshold allows investigation. Always restart services after changing amavisd. conf and monitor logs for errors pointing to syntax or socket problems. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Service start order and matching socket configuration are frequent causes of broken filtering. ClamAV and SpamAssassin must be running before Amavisd-new starts so Amavisd can connect to the scanners at launch. If Amavisd-new starts first and the scanner sockets are absent, Amavisd may log errors and fail to scan mail. The recommended restart order is: start or restart clamd (or clamd@scan), then spamassassin or spamd, then amavisd, and finally reload Postfix so it can send new mail through the content_filter. Another common pitfall is mismatched socket paths: clamd. conf defines LocalSocket or TCPSocket; that exact value must be referenced in amavisd. conf. If you see connection refused or missing socket errors in amavisd logs, confirm the socket path and permissions and check that the clamd socket file exists and is readable by the amavisd user. If you must run ClamAV on TCP, use 127.0.0.1:3310 in amavisd. conf. Also ensure firewall rules do not block loopback TCP if you rely on TCP sockets. Always inspect journalctl and maillog entries after restarts to detect timing issues. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Testing confirms the pipeline behaves as expected. For SpamAssassin you use the GTUBE string — a standard test pattern that triggers spam detection. For anti-virus you use the EICAR test file, which is harmless but recognized as malware by scanners. Choosing what to do with flagged mail depends on organizational risk tolerance and user expectations. For viruses, many administrators choose to reject infected mail outright by setting $final_virus_lovers to D_REJECT, because allowing infected attachments into inboxes risks compromise. For spam, options vary: you can tag and deliver, quarantine for administrator review, discard silently, or bounce. Use $sa_tag_level_kill and $sa_quarantine_cutoff_level to control when items are treated as spam and when they are quarantined. A typical mistake is setting aggressive thresholds that create many false positives; this harms users and increases support burden. Another mistake is over-trusting whitelists, which let potentially malicious mail bypass checks. A balanced policy is to quarantine high-scoring spam and tag medium scores so users can see warnings. Ensure quarantine notifications and retention policies are documented so administrators can find and restore mail if necessary. Whatever you choose, test the policy with GTUBE and EICAR and inspect logs to confirm the action is enforced. When filtering doesn't work, a methodical checklist reduces time to resolution. First, confirm services are running: systemctl status for clamd, spamassassin or spamd, and amavisd. Second, check Postfix main. cf to ensure content_filter is present; without it, Postfix will not send mail to Amavisd-new. Third, inspect master. cf for the returning listener on 127.0.0.1:10025 to ensure scanned mail is accepted back into Postfix with relaxed checks. Fourth, examine amavisd logs via journalctl -u amavisd for socket or syntax errors and maillog or journalctl for Postfix handoff and re-injection events. Fifth, verify ClamAV socket path and permissions; use ls -l on the socket file and match it to the path in amavisd. conf. Sixth, verify DNS resolution; SpamAssassin uses network lookups and may fail to apply rules without working DNS. Common mistakes include forgetting to reload Postfix after config changes, using the wrong socket path in amavisd. conf, and starting services in the wrong order. Work through the checklist, re-run tests, and keep a copy of original configurations for rollback. These are the core ideas to retain. Amavisd-new acts as the mediator between Postfix and scanners, enabling a manageable and scriptable scanning pipeline. SpamAssassin provides content scoring and tagging; use thresholds to decide when to tag, quarantine, or bounce messages. ClamAV performs attachment scanning; keep its signatures updated with freshclam and ensure the clamd socket configured in amavisd. conf matches clamd. conf. Postfix uses content_filter in main. cf to send mail for scanning and needs a matching listener in master. cf to receive scanned mail on 127.0.0.1:10025. Always start ClamAV and SpamAssassin before Amavisd-new, verify services are enabled and running, and test with GTUBE and EICAR strings while checking amavisd and mail logs.
